Our contributions are: an end-to-end GPU-accelerated integration of the five stages, with its kernel design documented; a GPU batch adaptation of Lien's $\varepsilon$-visibility with four custom CUDA kernels; a $β$-aware per-vehicle tour upper bound derived from the interpolated objective, supplementing the Desrochers-Laporte coefficient lift with forbidden-pair cuts; a 4D space-time extension of Zhou and Zeng's GPU parallel-frontier A*; and an experimental evaluation on 14 meshes (up to $7.2$M faces) that ablates the routing cuts and the parallel-frontier search, audits collision freedom and waypoint attainment \emph{after} trajectory smoothing, and measures the end-to-end gap against analytical and LP-relaxation lower bounds. Code and raw results are publicly available.

title: Sustainable and Envy-free Multi-Period Allocation
summary: Allocating renewable resources fairly requires accounting for how present decisions affect future availability. We introduce Sustainable and Envy-Free Multi-Period Allocation, in which agents are assigned over multiple periods to renewable resources whose quantities evolve over time according to renewal functions. An allocation must respect viability and capacity constraints while being envy-free over the whole time horizon. We study the computational and parameterized complexity of finding such allocations, with a focus on the three dimensions of the problem: the numbers of agents, resources, and periods. We show that finding such an allocation is NP-hard already for unary encoding and any single one of them being fixed to a constant. Whether two small dimensions suffice for tractability depends on the pair, the class of renewal functions, and the numerical encoding. For few resources and periods, binary-encoded instances remain hard in general, whereas unary encoding yields XP-time algorithms. For few resources and agents, binary-encoded instances also remain hard in general but become XP-time solvable when all renewal functions are translations. Few agents and periods yield fixed-parameter tractability, but no polynomial kernel under standard complexity assumptions.

title: FrontierRefactor: Benchmarking Multi-Scale Performance-Oriented Codebase Refactoring
summary: Autonomous codebase refactoring requires coding agents to restructure working software while strictly preserving externally observable behavior and prioritizing execution performance and compute efficiency over stylistic preference. Existing benchmarks: refactoring benchmarks assess functional correctness while overlooking runtime regressions, whereas code performance benchmarks target isolated micro-kernels that ignore codebase-scale complexity. We observe that refactoring scale is governed by the scope of the observable contract, the caller-visible interface fixing behavioral invariants while freeing private implementations for optimization. Building on this insight, we introduce FrontierRefactor, a benchmark of 60 qualified engineering tasks spanning four scales, from computational kernels to full repositories, across in-place optimization and cross-language rewriting. Evaluating frontier coding agents through a reference-free cascaded protocol across 1,080 execution runs reveals that correctness and speedup are largely decoupled: 41.2% of submissions satisfy functional equivalence yet fail to deliver verified performance improvements, with 19.3% suffering performance regressions and 21.9% trapped in measurement noise. Refactoring paradigms reveal orthogonal engineering bottlenecks: while cross-language rewrites gain speedups from native compilation after passing functional checks, agents struggle with contract fidelity, with pass rates dropping from 65.0% on modules to 32.6% at package scale; conversely, in-place optimization reliably preserves behavioral contracts at 86.5% but rarely achieves acceleration without physical performance profiling. Trajectory analysis shows that agents fall victim to uncalibrated micro-benchmarking illusions, an operational blind spot that multi-turn execution-timing feedback directly resolves, raising strict success from 16.0% to 40.0%.

title: How Effectively Do Security Skills Guide Coding Agents in Vulnerability Detection in Linux Kernel?
summary: Large language model (LLM) coding agents, such as Claude Code, are increasingly used for security auditing, with task-specific skills providing reusable vulnerability-analysis procedures. However, their effectiveness in detecting real vulnerabilities and the reasons for their failures remain unclear. We conduct the first large-scale empirical study of 37 security skills using Claude Code with four underlying LLMs on 100 real Linux kernel vulnerabilities across ten classes, totaling 14800 runs. We evaluate vulnerability detection at the function, statement, and vulnerability-class levels. Results show that 24.4 percent of runs locate the correct function, 18.3 percent identify both the function and responsible statement, and 15.7 percent correctly classify the vulnerability. Our failure analysis reveals limitations in evidence acquisition, state-relation reasoning, code interpretation, candidate verification, investigation coverage, and reporting. Based on these findings, we propose SKILL-SIF, a self-improving framework that iteratively evolves security skills by learning from missed vulnerabilities and failure patterns. We evolve five top-performing skills using the original benchmark and evaluate them on 100 previously unseen vulnerabilities. SKILL-SIF improves fully correct vulnerability detection by up to eight times (from 2 percent to 16 percent) on unseen vulnerabilities, while aggregate accuracy across four LLMs increases by 1.85 times (from 6.05 percent to 11.20 percent). These findings highlight the limitations of existing security skills and demonstrate the potential of failure-driven skill evolution to improve vulnerability detection in coding agents.

title: Conjugate Compilation: Self-Improving Agentic Co-Compilation for Speculative Decoding
summary: As LLM adoption surges, scaling model serving requires unlocking stranded GPU capacity alongside deploying more GPUs. Speculative decoding brings two models into the serving process: a small draft model proposes tokens that a larger target model verifies. Yet compiling these models individually leaves their shared execution outside the compiler's optimization boundary. We introduce CONJUGATE COMPILATION, which reframes speculative decoding as a cross-model compilation problem and jointly optimizes the draft and target models within their shared execution rather than treating each in isolation. Our key insight is that cross-model compilation should be informed by the measured performance of the co-located shared execution it produces: an optimization that improves a kernel in isolation need not improve the models when they execute together. To expand cross-model opportunities, we devise operand layouts that interleave blocks from both models within common tiles, co-locating GEMM and non-GEMM work while preserving their mathematics. We realize CONJUGATE COMPILATION through a self-improving agentic search system in which an LLM edits cross-model optimization plans using the compiler and GPU execution as its environment. Each proposed plan is compiled and evaluated through its co-located shared execution, whose measured score, together with kernel-level verdicts and compiler feedback, informs subsequent proposals, while Monte Carlo tree search accumulates rewards to guide exploration. Across six single-GPU speculative-decoding configurations on NVIDIA B300 and RTX 5090 GPUs, CONJUGATE COMPILATION achieves a geometric-mean per-round speedup of 1.37x over conventional execution. Interleaved kernels raise this speedup to 1.45x, reaching 1.59x in the best case. CONJUGATE COMPILATION also improves GPU utilization on average by 1.46x on RTX 5090 and 1.50x on B300.

title: EdgeKernelBench: Unified LLM-Driven Kernel Generation for Edge Backends
summary: Recent works show that LLMs can generate kernels with strong performance on server GPUs. Edge deployment presents distinct challenges because the hardware is heterogeneous, the software stacks are fragmented, and the resource budgets are tight. LLM kernel generation across diverse edge backends has yet to be studied systematically. We introduce EdgeKernelBench, which combines a unified IR deployment framework with a hierarchical benchmark for edge workloads. The unified IR captures reusable computation, scheduling, and memory decisions and connects to each target backend through a compiler interface. The benchmark spans progressively larger program scopes, from individual operators to compact model graphs, across representative edge application domains. We instantiate the design with TVM as a reference compiler and validate it across heterogeneous edge backends. With a single generation attempt, the best model achieves 64.5% Correct@1 but only 25.5% Fast@1.0. This gap shows that functional correctness does not consistently translate into performance gains. We therefore introduce the Layered Edge Kernel Agent (LEKA), which organizes optimization through a layered IR. On the agent evaluation subset, LEKA achieves 43.5% Fast@1.0, compared with 13.0% for direct generation and 26.1% for Claude Code. LEKA and Claude Code use the same base model and optimization budget. Together, EdgeKernelBench and LEKA support unified evaluation and layered optimization of kernels generated by LLMs across edge backends.

title: TCMScience: An Autonomous Scientist for Traditional Chinese Medicine
summary: Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) research connects classical texts, medicinal entities, molecular assays, computational predictions, and clinical studies. An autonomous research agent must preserve the inferential boundaries between these evidence types while coordinating analysis across heterogeneous resources. We introduce TCMScience, a scientific knowledge-discovery agent that separates language-model proposals from execution and release authority. Its architecture combines a trusted kernel, a scientific compiler, and claim-support contracts: plans are compiled into typed operations, execution is bounded by explicit permissions, and candidate findings are checked against source provenance, study design, and claim scope before release. The full capability registry contains 117 public-source connectors with 444 typed operations across 29 domains and 150 native tools across 12 domains; the TCM data hub catalogs 136 databases, 76 dataset specifications, and 84,294 formula-source records. These resources support model-independent workflows through browser and local execution interfaces. In a network-pharmacology analysis of Gegen Qinlian Tang, replacing the whole-proteome background with the assayed-protein background changed the number of significant pathways from 66 to zero; incorporating inactive screening records identified nine pathways, including drug-metabolism signals retained as mechanistic hypotheses. A governance ablation over 121 constructed erroneous outputs spanning 26 classes released 121 errors without governance, 57 with the domain layer, seven with the kernel, and zero with both layers. All 10 compliant controls were retained. These results establish complementary control of known failure modes and show how explicit evidence contracts change the conclusions an agent is permitted to report.

title: Proving LLM-Generated GPU Kernels Correct and Safe: Floating-Point Verification in Lean and VerCors
summary: Modern statistical model development begins with a high-level specification in an automatic differentiation framework such as PyTorch, JAX, or TensorFlow, which is then lowered to a target backend by a compiler or implemented manually by a research engineer. In this paper, we study whether frontier language models can correctly perform the latter task by generating GPU kernels from high-level benchmark specifications. We introduce a framework in which a language-model agent uses Velvet, a program verifier for imperative programs embedded in Lean, to prove semantic equivalence between a high-level specification and a generated CUDA kernel under an explicit set of assumptions. It also asks the LLM to prove thread safety and data race freedom of the generated kernel in VerCors, a deductive verifier for parallel code. Our main contribution to the formal verification of LLM- generated GPU kernels is showing that a combination of Lean automation and language-model-guided proof construction can verify a broad set of basic neural- network building blocks over floating-point values, allowing LLMs to implement semantically correct and safe kernels. In our framework, floating-point verifications never rely on compiled code and are always checked via the Lean kernel.

title: Organon : From Evolutionary Search to Recursive Self-Improving Agents for Scientific Discovery
summary: Scientific discovery does not follow a single fixed methodology: research methods vary across domains and evolve through experimentation as investigations unfold. Although LLM-guided evolutionary search has advanced automated discovery, existing frameworks typically rely on fixed search procedures or restrict adaptation to predefined components, limiting their ability to address diverse research problems and adapt to challenges that emerge at runtime. We introduce Organon, a recursively self-improving agent for scientific discovery. During execution, a single persistent agent analyzes its accumulated experience and autonomously revises its own search strategies, population management, diagnostic tools, memory, and worker coordination. These revisions take effect at runtime, allowing the agent to continuously adapt its approach as research progresses. Importantly, the agent can also diagnose and correct flaws in its own adaptation procedures, enabling recursive improvement of the mechanisms that guide its future self-improvement. We evaluate Organon across 21 computational discovery tasks spanning algorithm design, GPU kernel optimization, mathematical construction, and systems optimization. On ALE-Bench Lite, Organon achieves the best performance among competing search frameworks on all 10 tasks, improving mean held-out performance by 20.5% over EvoX. On KernelBench, it achieves the best results on three of four workloads, with speedups of up to 1.67x over the strongest competing method. Analysis of the search trajectories further reveals how the agent develops task-specific search strategies, builds new diagnostic capabilities, and corrects or reverses its own earlier revisions. We implement Organon using DeepSeek Harness and Cordis's spatiotemporal composability. Code is available at https://github.com/cheikh025/Organon.

title: An exact finite-state representation of viscoelastic memory for accelerated sea-level modeling: SLEvolve v1.0
summary: Glacial Isostatic Adjustment (GIA) models solve the gravitationally self-consistent sea-level equation for the response of the solid Earth and the oceans to changing ice loads. As these models are increasingly embedded in coupled ice-sheet simulations, glacial-cycle calculations, and large ensembles, standard pseudo-spectral 1-D solvers face a steep computational barrier: they evaluate the viscoelastic response by explicitly re-summing every past load increment, scaling quadratically with time steps as $O(N^2)$. Here we show that this computational penalty is an artifact of algorithmic formulation rather than Earth physics. By exploiting the exponential form of the viscoelastic relaxation kernel, we reformulate the viscous response as an exact recursive update of a finite set of modal states, without re-summing the load history. This exact reformulation alone reduces the cost of a run to $O(N)$, yielding a 20.6-fold speed-up relative to a standard full-history 1-D GIA solver for a case study involving a 550-step Antarctic future sea-level projection. Implemented in our open-source solver SLEvolve v1.0, this formulation---combined with fewer, table-free and multithreaded spherical-harmonic transforms, improved file handling, and physics-inspired iteration starts---achieves an end-to-end speed-up of over three orders of magnitude (up to 4,000-fold) against the same 1-D GIA solver, reducing day-long simulations to under thirty seconds on a workstation. Beyond this solid-Earth application, SLEvolve illustrates how human-derived analytical reformulations can be combined with benchmark-harnessed AI-assisted engineering to modernize scientific software. In particular, Numerical regression tests and performance profiling guided the AI agents' implementation choices and helped reject ineffective optimizations.

title: HardEval: An Execution-Verified Benchmark for AI-Driven Security Hardening and Compliance Remediation
summary: Implementing Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG) controls remains a demanding operating-system administration task. Each natural-language security requirement must be translated into a precise and persistent configuration change. These changes span Secure Shell (SSH) configuration, authentication policy, audit rules, and kernel parameters. Existing benchmarks do not measure whether a model can perform this task on a live system. Code benchmarks evaluate isolated programs without persistent system state, while agent benchmarks largely focus on applications rather than operating-system configuration. In this paper, we introduce \textbf{HardEval}, an execution-verified benchmark for evaluating language-model-assisted security hardening. HardEval is built from Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8 STIG controls that fail on an unhardened baseline system. Expert-written reference remediations and Open Vulnerability and Assessment Language (OVAL) checks serve as hidden ground truth for grading; they are never shown to the model, and each task states only the required security outcome while withholding the implementation. The model produces a Bash script, which is executed on a live virtual machine and graded from fail to pass using the corresponding OpenSCAP/OVAL compliance check. Evaluation of fourteen frontier and open-weight configurations reveals large and uneven capability differences across security domains. A recurring failure mode is plausible security code that does not satisfy the exact compliance condition. For four open-weight configurations, multi-run Wilson confidence intervals preserve the observed ordering. HardEval is publicly available.

title: AgentLoupe: Kernel-Resident Semantic Causal Labels for AI Agent Observability
summary: AI agents translate user intents into system actions via tool invocations. Accurately attributing these actions to their originating LLM interactions is essential for security auditing, yet existing methods, such as AgentSight, fail for delayed execution and cross-process-lineage behaviors. We present AgentLoupe, an application-transparent eBPF-based observability tool. The core insight of AgentLoupe is to embed causal identity into kernel resources. AgentLoupe employs eBPF to capture TLS plaintext to interpret LLM interactions, and assigns each a kernel-resident semantic label. It maintains labels in eBPF maps, then propagates this label across processes and threads, associates it with kernel resources such as files and sockets. When a persistent resource carries context to an independent process outside the original lineage, this design preserves the delayed causal association. Experiments show that the average observation overhead of AgentLoupe is below 8%, and case studies confirm AgentLoupe traces cross-lineage persistent attacks back to their originating LLM interactions.

title: Architecting for Hardware Diversity: Meta's End-to-End Co-Design for High-Performance AI Training on AMD GPUs
summary: Meta deploys a heterogeneous fleet comprising NVIDIA GPUs, AMD GPUs, and proprietary MTIA accelerators to reduce costs and mitigate vendor lock-in. However, the extensive history of NVIDIA-specific optimizations hinders performance portability to other hardware. This paper presents our methods for optimizing alternative accelerators, using AMD Instinct MI350X versus NVIDIA B200 for recommendation model training as a case study. We propose three reusable principles. First, hardware-model co-design is essential: rather than directly porting models from NVIDIA GPUs, revising model structures and software recipes allows full exploitation of accelerator-specific strengths (e.g., MI350X's 1.6x HBM capacity relative to B200). Second, our analytical performance model enables zero-warmup optimal kernel selection across diverse datatypes and matrix shapes in production models, drastically simplifying tuning. Third, increasingly mature agentic workflows have lowered the barrier to porting from the CUDA ecosystem; we extend these workflows for microarchitecture-aware kernel optimizations and custom shim generation. Compared to the directly ported baseline, these methods deliver up to 1.5x improvement in end-to-end training throughput. To our knowledge, this is the first hyperscaler report on productionizing AMD GPUs for large-scale training. Our contributions have been upstreamed to the open-source PyTorch, Triton, and ROCm ecosystems.

title: Benchmarking and Enhancing Design-Aware Code Review in the Linux Kernel
summary: Code review often requires reasoning beyond local correctness. In mature software systems, reviewers must recognize design trade-offs introduced by a proposed change, compare alternative solutions, and reason about their compatibility with project-specific constraints. We refer to this problem as design-aware code review. However, existing automated review approaches primarily focus on defects and correctness, while the design knowledge accumulated in historical review discussions remains difficult to reuse. To address these challenges, we present DesignLore, a knowledge-augmented approach that extracts design decisions from historical review discussions, organizes them into an adaptive design taxonomy, and reuses relevant historical knowledge to guide code review. We further construct DesignReviewBench, a benchmark derived from real patch-review histories for systematically evaluating design-aware code review. Our evaluation shows that design-aware review remains challenging for current coding agents, with the strongest baseline achieving an F1 of only 0.213 on design trade-off detection. In comparison, DesignLore achieves an F1 of 0.259, a 21.6% relative improvement, and consistently delivers gains across different agent systems and backbone. These results highlight the importance of design-aware review and demonstrate the potential of recovering and reusing historical design knowledge to support it.

title: Kernel-Based Heterogeneous Mean Field Games on a Continuum Type Space
summary: This paper studies a class of heterogeneous mean field games on a continuum type space, in which interactions are generated by a Hilbert-Schmidt kernel operator acting on the type-indexed mean state profile. The control set is allowed to be a general closed convex subset of a Euclidean space, and the optimal feedback is characterized through the unique maximizer of the Hamiltonian. For a prescribed mean-field path, the stochastic maximum principle leads to a family of fully coupled forward-backward stochastic differential equations (FBSDEs) indexed by the agent type. Under Lipschitz conditions and a monotonicity assumption on the reduced coefficients, the frozen FBSDE is globally well posed. We then formulate the consistency problem as a fixed-point problem for the kernel mean-field path. When the operator norm of the interaction kernel is sufficiently small, the resulting map has an invariant ball and is continuous and compact, so that Schauder's theorem yields existence of a mean field Nash equilibrium. Uniqueness follows under an aggregate monotonicity condition adapted to the kernel coupling. A linear-quadratic example illustrates how finite-rank interactions and heterogeneous risk preferences produce coupled collective modes, and yields a spectral smallness condition for existence and an explicit sufficient condition for uniqueness.

title: Scaling Discovery Requires Forgetting
summary: Automated research with LLM agents has shown promising results in various domains. Through iterative refinement and scored verifiers, LLM agents are capable of discovering new ideas. There are different ways to scale automated research: let one agent iterate for longer, run several agents in parallel, or further let the parallel agents communicate and build on one another's candidates. However, we find that all three strategies eventually plateau as the agents accumulate history. Each agent becomes anchored to its own past attempts, making fewer and smaller edits. Beyond this point, additional budget brings little further improvement. In this paper, we show that the key to scaling discovery further is to forget. Periodically discarding the search state, including every agent's session and the candidate history, and restarting from the best candidate found so far, unblocks the search and pushes the same budget further. We implement forgetting in a team of agents with communication and evaluate it on four tasks spanning heuristic programming, kernel optimization and model training. The results show up to 15% improvement compared to parallel agents, and up to 39% compared to a single agent. Our results suggest that, for open-ended discovery, what an agent is allowed to remember matters as much as how much compute it is given.

title: HPCAgent-Bench: A Framework for Sound Benchmarking of Code-Optimizing Agents, Harnesses, and Skills
summary: Coding agents are increasingly used to optimize code, but existing benchmarks fix one accelerator, programming model or harness, so they cannot isolate what each component contributes or show whether added skills and tools repay their cost. We present HPCAgent-Bench with 689 kernels in three tracks: loop-level optimization challenges, kernels extracted from HPC codes, and machine-learning models. The framework specifies each kernel once in NumPy, derives C and Fortran references, accepts submissions through a common C ABI or Python interface, and runs them on CPUs or GPUs, on one or multiple nodes. An external judge checks correctness on hidden fuzzed inputs and times each submission, closing paths agents use to exploit the testing system. We introduce two metrics for reporting results: \textit{intervention efficacy} measures an intervention, such as adding a tool, through paired runs on speedup, success rate and cost, and \textit{weighted token cost} reports input, cached-input and output tokens under explicit weights. Agents reach up to $4.2\times$ speedup over automatic parallelizers, and their optimizations transfer to another machine: $93$--$99\%$ of answers without device-specific code remain correct, and per-kernel speedups keep a rank correlation of $r_s\ge0.84$. Across 40 matched setups, interventions significantly change speedup only twice but token cost by up to $3.0\times$. Because token weighting decides whether a saving is significant, we state the weights and release every token count as a standard for cost reporting. We provide the first comprehensive, broad and hardened benchmark for the sound evaluation of agentic optimization, with transparent cost metrics.

title: Verifying deployed bytecode against executable EVM semantics, with exact gas and no added axioms
summary: Much of Ethereum's most consequential code is immutable bytecode: old output of unverified compilers, and protocol logic run as contract code. We show that such bytecode can be verified as it is, without trusting what produced it, without simplifying the machine it runs on, and with no axioms beyond Lean's own. Blanc, a Lean 4 verification stack, reads fixed runtime bytes via kernel-checked certificates and states every theorem against Jaune, an executable semantics of the EVM and block processing that passes all 34,205 blockchain-test cases of Ethereum's fixture release v20.0.2 that involve only forks that have governed mainnet since May 2025. Eight artifacts, deployed from 2017 to 2026, come from seven compiler versions and an assembler. For the EIP-7002 contract, we prove that the end-of-block call to it, whose failure would invalidate the block, succeeds whatever its storage holds, and that each block's withdrawal requests are exactly the oldest pending submissions; mainnet met these theorems' starting premises when Prague began. For a Uniswap V2 pair, we prove that after any valid history whose hashed slots stay apart, from any checkpoint representing its Solidity model's state, the storage represents that model replayed over exactly the committed calls, a balanced liquidity ledger stays balanced, and, under a premise on token answers, geometric-mean reserves per share fall only through the protocol fee. Exact gas makes liveness provable: a tracked WETH9 holder without code can withdraw by a transaction whose gas has a closed form, matching all 3,748 comparable mainnet receipts of its shape in 30,000 blocks. On Curve pool bytes compiled with the lock bug exploited in 2023, Jaune executes such a reentrancy from deployment; for bytes from a fixed compiler, we prove the lock excludes it. AI agents wrote the proofs in fifteen days under one author's direction, atop an existing stack.

title: L3M: A Verifiable Harness and Runtime for Self-Extending and Self-Improving Agents
summary: The lasting gains in AI have come from methods that absorb more computation, and language models already scale computation within a call. Useful work, though, happens across calls: over hours or days, through tools and external systems, among many agents and the humans they work for, and increasingly through code the agents write themselves. Whether that work compounds is enabled by the harness around it, and the harness faces a constraint the model does not: of the three participants in such a computation, the human, the model and code, only the human's attention does not scale, so the computation can grow only if the human is not in every loop. L3M is a runtime built on that premise, written in Lean 4 so that one language implements the harness, states its invariants, and is the language agents extend it in. One computation spans humans, agents, models and code, and all of its state lives in Git: a rich state trajectory -- rather than a chat conversation -- is an object the runtime can resume, rewind, fork, compare and merge. Waiting, communication, delegation and undo are primitives, not patterns the model reasons through each time. When an agent works out a procedure, it can write it once as a sealed Lean program whose type is its permission request, and the harness offers it back as a tool -- machinery for the model to use. To take the human out of the loop, L3M uses reversibility to decide where that is safe: a tool's review tier follows from how far its effects can be undone, so agents act freely where the runtime can recover. Because the machinery can change, the properties that make this safe are stated as kernel-checked theorems about the code that runs. On Terminal-Bench, an untuned L3M reaches about two thirds of its (unsafe) shell-equipped pass rate using only safe (not needing human review) tools.

title: Beyond the Trial-and-Error Loop: Hybrid Projection and Automated Tuning for Distributed Training
summary: Configuring distributed LLM training across hundreds of GPUs requires jointly optimizing tensor, pipeline, expert, context, and data parallelism alongside micro-batch size, recomputation, sharding, and overlap, a combinatorial space where memory legality can hinge on a single byte of activation accounting. Today, teams navigate it through expensive multi-node trial and error, burning GPU-hours on crashes and suboptimal recipes. We present Primus Projection, which closes this loop with two coupled components. First, a hybrid projection engine that measures what it can and simulates what it cannot: GPU microbenchmarks on as few as a single device capture compute kernels and any in-scope communication; a sub-node downscale-measure-upscale workflow analytically restores out-of-scope collectives, FSDP overlap, and the full pipeline schedule at the multi-node target. A pure simulation mode runs entirely on CPU, enabling pre-silicon planning without any GPU. Second, the Primus Tuning Agent treats the projection engine as a fast scoring oracle (seconds per candidate instead of tens of minutes) and uses it to drive an intelligent search over the configuration space. A deterministic seed planner sweeps single axes; an LLM investigation loop proposes cross-axis combinations the planner cannot reach, with an analytic memory pre-filter that rejects infeasible candidates before any GPU time is spent. Validated on Llama 3.1 (dense) and Mixtral 8x22B (MoE) across two GPU generations, all projections stay within ~10% of measured multi-node throughput, and fidelity holds at production scale: 4.7% error on DeepSeek V3 671B at 1,024 GPUs and 1.9% on Qwen3-235B-A22B at 256 GPUs. In a Mixtral 8x22B case study, the Primus Tuning Agent discovers a configuration delivering +27% throughput over the published 4-node BF16 reference at the same scale, in under 30 minutes of single-node exploration.

title: AReaL-RSI: Adaptive Scaling and Coordination of Recursive Self-Improvement
summary: Scaling recursive self-improvement requires additional computation to produce useful research progress in reaching persistent objectives. Intuitively, more researcher agents can explore more hypotheses, but early evaluation scores might misrepresent their promise, shared findings could lose their applicability conditions, and useful procedures could remain confined to completed investigations. In this paper, we present AReaL-RSI, a framework for organizing a persistent research team of agents without updating backbone LLM weights. We formulate the scaling problem in terms of evaluated outcomes and whole-system resource expenditure. Concretely, a leader agent selects task-appropriate research orientations and guides ongoing investigations; conditional memory sharing distinguishes unresolved problems from supported findings and enables recipient adaptation. During recursive evolution, after each campaign, evidence-based review revises researcher orientation, knowledge, and skills for later campaigns. Experiments compare AReaL-RSI with Codex-Goal on downstream harness optimization, GPU kernel optimization, and AI research tasks using two backbones. Under the reported resource allocations, AReaL-RSI improves Terminal Bench performance by 2.2 percentage points for each backbone and increases mean KernelBench speedup by 32.2-36.8%; further scalability comparisons favor the design of AReaL-RSI over native scaling: combining experience sharing with specialized researcher roles yields 1.9-27.5% lower kernel latency than independent exploration and 1.3-33.9% lower latency than sharing alone across all seven comparable task-backbone pairs.

title: Gaussian Process Bandits for AI System Optimization with Selectively Verified Feedback
summary: Gaussian process bandits exploit similarities among configurations to optimize prompts, retrieval systems, and agent workflows. In these applications, however, inexpensive model-based evaluations can disagree with trusted task outcomes. We study selective verification when an action is chosen before a diagnostic is observed and trusted feedback is informative on an unknown set of diagnostic states. A finite reliability class and a finite RKHS signal dictionary describe these two sources of uncertainty. We construct a fixed audit design that combines reliability coverage with reward separation and establish a finite-time regret bound that accounts for a hard audit budget and the rounds needed to obtain informative observations. A safe adaptive extension mixes this robust design with predictable Chernoff allocations while preserving a uniform identification floor and exact expected acquisition-cost accounting. For signed-coordinate kernels, structured and diffuse reliability classes require different audit scales despite sharing the same reward geometry. Synthetic experiments distinguish these certified designs from an adaptive posterior heuristic and GP controls. Safe adaptive allocation reduces aggregate regret relative to the fixed design under the exact dictionary, but its finite-budget error certificate is numerically loose. Conditional-feedback errors can remove the heuristic's advantage and target perturbations can reverse it. Separate AI-task replays assess feedback correction and fitted-dictionary policies without establishing end-to-end validation of a learned selective-verification method.

title: ATTUNE: Agentic Throughput Tuning for LLM Training
summary: Training a large language model can occupy thousands of GPUs for weeks, and its speed depends on its recipe: how the model is split across GPUs, how memory is traded for compute, and which kernels and communication overlaps it uses. Finding a good recipe is still manual work for experts. Automated tuners search fixed lists of knobs and check only that a job runs, so they miss large gains and can ship changes that silently alter what the model learns. ATTUNE tunes any working recipe unattended within a GPU-hour budget. A coding agent, guided by lessons from past tuning runs, finds each run's bottleneck and changes one setting at a time, and a correctness gate outside the agent refuses changes known to alter training. ATTUNE is deployed in production at Amazon Ads, a business that reported $19.8 billion in revenue in Q2 2026. Its recipes train the models that power Amazon's Ads Agent. On three of the models it tunes, its recipes raise throughput per GPU by 1.7x on average and up to 3.9x over internal expert-tuned recipes. It also speeds up four of NVIDIA's benchmark recipes by 7-26% and held-out public recipes by up to 2.6x, and beats Bayesian optimization, random search and OptiCo, a recent LLM-agent tuner, at the same GPU-hour budget. We release ATTUNE at github.com/amazon-science/attune and OpenRecipes, a leaderboard of more than 60 verified recipes, at openrecipes.ai.

title: DuoDiscover: Scaling Autonomous Discovery Beyond the Evaluation Bottleneck
summary: Evaluation has been central to advances in AI, and it is equally critical to autonomous discovery. Yet scaling autonomous discovery to real-world engineering challenges faces a fundamental bottleneck: the cost of evaluating progress. In real settings, a single true evaluation, such as a full benchmark or serving trace, can take hours, so a search can afford only a handful of true evaluations. We present DuoDiscover, a search system that jointly discovers what to optimize and how to evaluate progress efficiently, through three mechanisms. First, each worker in a fleet of coding agents co-discovers an optimization target and a fast, tailored proxy evaluator, which we call a yardstick. The agent then hill-climbs the yardstick rather than the true evaluation. Second, since search can exploit gaps between a yardstick and the true objective, fidelity tests continually recheck each yardstick's ranking and invalidate any that drift. Third, the fleet is bottom-up, with no central decomposition of the problem. A lightweight orchestrator spawns and terminates agents, briefs running ones, and seeds new agents with others' confirmed work. DuoDiscover enables autonomous optimization from software to chip architecture. We demonstrate DuoDiscover on two repository-level benchmarks and four GPU and TPU kernel suites covering hundreds of kernels. On SWE-fficiency, it doubles the average speedup of human experts. On SOL-Exec, it ranks first on 121 of 235 kernels and in the top three on 212. On the heavily optimized vLLM and SQLite engines, DuoDiscover achieves 1.92$\times$ and 1.38$\times$ gains over the base code. On a CPU microarchitecture optimization task with evaluations of up to 28 hours, DuoDiscover surpasses both AlphaEvolve-based ArchAgent v2 and the best human design, with 1.65$\times$ ArchAgent v2's gain in 16.7 days versus more than 40 days, advancing the frontier of autonomous chip design.

title: Controller-Agnostic Runtime Safety Certificates for Tool-Using AI Agents via Data-Driven Robust Reachability
summary: Software agents built on large language models act by issuing tool calls, some of which cannot be undone. To control theory the model is an opaque feedback controller, replaced every few months, whose closed loop cannot be analyzed directly. We propose a runtime filter, or shield, between any such controller and its environment that certifies a bound on the probability of reaching an unsafe condition during a bounded task. Given a predicate abstraction and candidate successor sets, everything else comes from logs: the loop becomes a finite controlled Markov chain, the estimated kernel is surrounded by a distribution-free confidence region, and robust reach-avoid value iteration runs over it. The certificate is probably approximately correct and uniform over controllers respecting the filter, so one model may replace another without recomputation. In all tested datasets the true risk stayed within certificate and budget; in a file-system sandbox the filter stays sound against a hazard the logs barely covered, where a plug-in baseline certifies safety and fails; and it holds seven controllers, three of them open-weights models, to zero unsafe outcomes in 1050 episodes.

title: Small but Mighty: Test Suites as Improvement Signals for Self-Evolving Agents
summary: A self-evolving agent rewrites its own harness and must decide which rewrites to keep, so its improvement signal is the check a rewrite has to pass. Verifying a rewrite by agent rollout is expensive and subjective, while executable checks such as the repository's own tests are too sparse to catch behavior-changing rewrites, rejecting only a quarter of them. We instead take test feedback as the executable signal, and search for test suites that are both small and strong with a quality-diversity evolutionary algorithm, so that the signal is dense and informative. TeSearch treats suite size as a behavior descriptor, so that quality is pursued at every size and a small, strong suite is reachable, and learns a transition kernel during the search that denoises the LLM as an actuator on that descriptor. Across 129 real-world modules and three backbones, TeSearch delivers the highest-quality suites of any method compared, LLM-driven evolutionary search included, and the smallest of any LLM-based one. Used as the improvement signal of a self-evolving agent, it rejects 59.9% of behavior-changing rewrites against 25.3% for the repository's tests, at a 4.0% false-alarm rate and 3.5 s per decision. The code and data are available at https://github.com/ccsnow127/TeSearch.

title: TenonAgent: Virtualizing Execution Residency for Memory-Oversubscribed LLM Agents
summary: LLM agents execute as long-lived, multi-stage workflows with substantial resource-demand variation across phases. Provisioning each agent or sandbox for its lifetime peak leads to low resource utilization, particularly for memory, whereas aggressive oversubscription risks memory contention, out-of-memory failures, and costly workflow retries. This tension limits the concurrency and efficiency of agent serving under constrained host memory. We present TenonAgent, a runtime system that virtualizes sandbox residency by decoupling the logical agent's lifetime from its physical execution environment. To manage memory oversubscription, TenonAgent employs a dual-timescale control plane. At action boundaries, it combines predictive admission control with a fail-closed, restart-safe contract, dynamically materializing or dematerializing sandboxes based on global memory pressure. During active tool execution, a sched_ext-based kernel gate paces sandbox execution permissions to reduce unexpected concurrent memory growth. The gate provides feedback control over future execution opportunities. Evaluations across diverse agentic workloads show that, under the tested workloads and parameter settings, TenonAgent substantially reduces observed OOM failures and achieves a 100% task success rate in bursts reaching an 8.6x memory oversubscription ratio. Overall, it delivers up to a 5.5x speedup over unmanaged execution, outperforms existing agent-level and cgroup-based schedulers by 5x to 37x, and provides consistent benefits across both Docker and Firecracker microVM backends.

title: TileCas: Cascading Kernel Development Across Programming Abstractions
summary: Programming abstractions have traditionally been designed for humans, but code generation is increasingly performed by models and autonomous agents. We investigate abstractions for machine-driven programming through GPU and AI-accelerator kernel generation. High-level domain-specific languages (DSLs) simplify search by delegating implementation details to compilers, while lower-level representations provide finer-grained control at the cost of a larger and more complex search space. In this paper, we present TileCas, a unified, pluggable interface that enables coding agents to develop kernels across multiple editable abstraction levels. Rather than committing to a single representation, TileCas allows an agent to transfer and refine candidates across levels through Cross-Level Diagnosis, which maps correctness and performance feedback to actionable controls at different abstraction levels; Abstraction Scheduling, which selects both the candidate and representation from which subsequent refinement should proceed; and a Heterogeneous Search Tree, which preserves and revisits alternative search trajectories spanning multiple representations. We integrate TileCas with two code agents AKO and KDA, and evaluate both integrations on 50 end-to-end KernelBench Level 3 workloads across two accelerator platforms and two language models. Giving equal weight to the four accelerator-model configurations, AKO with TileCas achieves an arithmetic-mean speedup of $4.84\times$, compared with $3.75\times$ for the strongest evaluated baseline without TileCas, an improvement of 29.0%. Integrating the same interface with KDA improves its mean speedup by 69.2%, with gains in every configuration. These results show that allowing coding agents to navigate across programming abstractions can improve machine-driven software development and can be reused across different base workflows.

title: No, Your Tools Are Not Enough: It's Time to Bring Agents to the Hunt
summary: Modern software systems are large and complex, demanding scalable and autonomous techniques for vulnerability discovery. Existing approaches still depend on human expertise for domain knowledge, and on human intervention throughout the process of vulnerability discovery. AI agents offer us an opportunity to make vulnerability discovery more adaptive, scalable, and autonomous. Agents bring the ability to make continuous decisions and adapt, and general knowledge that can be augmented. In this paper, we present our experience using AI agents to find vulnerabilities across diverse programs such as Windows drivers, the Linux kernel, XNU, firmware, and web applications. We use an iterative agentic workflow and find that it generalizes across these targets. We discuss tasks that agents help with, which were previously challenging, and some future research directions we consider important for advancing autonomous vulnerability discovery.

title: Names Are Not Objects: Object-Bound Confinement for Compromised AI Coding Agents
summary: Coding agents read repositories and web pages that anyone can write, and then act with their user's authority. Prompt-injection defenses make it less likely that the model is steered but do not prevent it, so the system around the model must contain an agent that is already compromised. Many exploits against deployed coding agents share one cause: a check approves a name, such as a path, an argument vector, or a directory, and a later step maps that name to a different object: the file behind a symlink, the behavior an option selects, or a repository that git discovers on its own. We present Zero-Trust Agent Cells (ZTAC). A cell runs the agent in a kernel sandbox whose only route to files, programs, and the network is a socket to a broker. The broker resolves each request to the object it will act on, decides on that object, and checks at use that it is acting on the object it authorized. Programs that the broker starts run in a sandbox compiled from the same policy, and approvals are bound to the resolved object and can be used once. Our macOS prototype has 3.2k lines of trusted Rust code, excluding dependencies. We evaluate it against 74 attacks with ground-truth oracles, including replays of 10 publicly disclosed incidents. A tool allowlist loses 66 of them, and an allowlist combined with the kind of command sandbox that deployed agents use loses 56. ZTAC loses 2, both of which encode a secret into traffic to an allowed endpoint, and holds 14 for review. It completes 43 of 46 benign operations, with 8 approval prompts, and 4 of 7 workflows. A no-op brokered request has a median latency of 4.0 ms, and the spawned programs we measured take 8.5 ms to 18.4 ms longer than without ZTAC.

title: AutoEnvScaling: Automating the Data Flywheel with Terminal Agents
summary: Terminal agents solve tasks in software engineering and scientific research by executing commands in a terminal. Training them via reinforcement learning (RL) requires diverse and verifiable environments, but these environments are still mostly designed by human researchers, so their supply grows only as fast as researchers can work. We introduce AutoEnvScaling, which treats environment design as a terminal task and uses agents to automate the data flywheel. A proposer agent builds new RL environments from the rollouts of the solver being trained, and the solver's new rollouts guide the next round. By turning environment generation into a terminal task, AutoEnvScaling increases the valid-environment rate by up to 25 times compared to prompt-only generation, at up to 75% lower cost per valid environment. We show that training Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on AutoEnvScaling environments from GPT-5.6-sol improves its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score by 4.3 points over the matched Tmax baseline. The broader goal of AutoEnvScaling is to enable recursive self-improvement (RSI): by making both environment generation and solving terminal tasks, it lets one model co-evolve in both roles. We show that Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, acting in both roles, gains 12.2 points on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and raises its Terminal-Bench 4.0 score from 1.6 to 3.2. The pipeline also generalizes across agentic domains, generating environments for software engineering, computer use, professional work, and GPU kernel programming. Overall, these results show a path toward agents building their own training environments, reducing human reliance and taking a core step toward RSI.

title: Probabilistic Ship Trajectory Forecasting using Transformer Models on AIS Data
summary: Anticipation of vessel trajectories is an essential task when navigating at sea. This applies to both human navigators and autonomous surface vessels. Trajectory forecasting enables sub-routines such as collision avoidance to assess the situation and react accordingly in time. This paper investigates Transformer and Performer models for trajectory prediction of surface vessels in confined waters. Using widely available position data from the Automatic Identification System (AIS), candidate models are trained and evaluated. Historical information on how other vessels have moved in the local area surrounding each agent is conveyed using positional heat maps. The heat maps are generated using Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) and encoded with a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) before entering the Transformer models. The models are trained with quantile loss to efficiently obtain a model-aware prediction interval, as this is crucial for timely collision avoidance. The proposed model architectures are shown to greatly outperform previous work while the inclusion of local heat maps enables the prediction of vessel movement that is not otherwise indicated from the previous positions.

title: Humanize MLE Agents: Multi-Agent Session Alternation Beyond Single-Agent Limits
summary: Existing LLM-based agent approaches for long-horizon machine learning engineering (MLE) often use context engineering, implemented through custom harnesses that manage tools, skills, and accumulated experience. However, we find that as single-session execution lengthens, the agent's reasoning intensity declines alongside slowing progress, summarized as long-horizon deceleration, and the benefits of these custom harnesses vanish as the underlying model improves, summarized as harness staleness. These findings suggest that their benefits may not persist across versions, which motivates a workflow-level approach in which agents build on one another's work across sessions. We model these alternating agent sessions as a context-reset semi-Markov decision process (CR-SMDP) and establish sufficient conditions for alternation to exceed single-agent reference limits, derive an explicit experiment-budget bound, and characterize when session caps preserve this advantage. Guided by this analysis, we introduce Humanize MLE Agents (HMA), which alternates two agents on a shared workspace, limits each session to at most k experiments and resets the context between sessions, without additional task-specific harness or prior knowledge supplements. Across 75 Kaggle tasks in MLE-bench, HMA reaches a state-of-the-art any-medal rate of 78.2%, exceeding the strongest open-source baseline by 8.0 points with a quarter of its time budget. Moreover, among six configurations spanning five heterogeneous agent pairs, HMA improves any-medal rate over the constituent baselines by 6.4 points on average, demonstrating cross-pair generality. A supplementary case on kernel optimization reaches 878 cycles, within 1.6% of the community leaderboard leader, demonstrating applicability beyond MLE.

title: SqueezeBench: Saturation-Resilient Evaluation of Mathematical Capability
summary: AI systems are making rapid progress in mathematics, but this progress is hard to measure. Benchmarks of solved problems saturate, and in benchmarks of open problems each problem can be resolved for the first time only once. We present SqueezeBench, a benchmark that is resilient to saturation: a success raises the bar instead of removing the problem. Each problem fixes an integer function $f(n)$ whose values are known only for small $n$, and the benchmark keeps a lower and an upper record on it. A record is a computable Lean function with a machine-checked proof that it bounds $f$. A submission proposes a new function and proves that it bounds $f$, that it is no worse than the current record at any $n$, and that it is strictly better at some $n$. Once accepted, it becomes the record that the next submission has to beat. The system thus chooses the bound as well as its proof, and it may improve the record at a single $n$ or its growth rate. At every $n$, the gap between the two records shows how far the certified bounds are from determining $f(n)$. Every proof is checked by two independent Lean kernels, so no referee needs to check the mathematics. The checks also reject a function that computes $f$ by exhaustive search at small $n$, and a maintainer only reads the submitter's report and looks for such a search at larger $n$. We release ten problems from extremal combinatorics with twenty proved initial records and the admission tools. As a baseline, agents based on a frontier language model, with at most one hour per record, had 82 submissions accepted and improved every record, without going beyond the published literature. Agents based on two newer models then started from these records, had 60 more submissions accepted and improved 19 of the 20 records again. For eight of the ten problems, at least one record is still asymptotically behind the best published bound.

title: Compaction-Aware Reinforcement Learning For Ascend Triton Kernel Generation
summary: Automatically generating high-performance kernels with LLM-based agents promises substantial gains in development efficiency, but two obstacles remain. First, while increasing multi-turn interaction with execution environments is crucial for refining generation quality, continuous context accumulation rapidly exceeds the model's effective context window. Second, training long-horizon tasks via GRPO inherently incurs sparse rewards due to its reliance on terminal outcome evaluation, severely hindering step-level credit assignment; To address these obstacles, we propose ATRL (Ascend Triton Reinforcement Learning), a post-training method that refines GRPO into a compaction-aware, segment-level objective for long-horizon kernel generation. We also design a lightweight agent harness providing cascaded compilation, correctness, and profiling feedback, alongside an Ascend-specific knowledge base injected during agentic RL training and evaluation to compensate for the base model's missing platform expertise. Evaluations on NPUKernelBench and KernelBench, both executed on Ascend hardware, show that ATRL consistently surpasses all baselines, including GRPO, in both correctness and speedup.

title: VortexSynth: Profile-guided benchmark reconstruction for GPU architecture research
summary: GPU architecture research requires representative benchmarks that can execute on new designs. However, many vendor-tailored workloads and library kernels cannot run directly on research architectures because their implementations are closed-source or rely on programming models unsupported by the target architecture. Migrating existing kernels requires manual effort to adapt their implementations and validate their behavior. This creates a need to automate workload migration to target platforms. We present VortexSynth, a framework that uses profile-guided benchmark reconstruction to construct GPU benchmarks from reference workloads. Our workflow selects hot kernels through profiling, synthesizes implementations in the target programming language, verifies output equivalence, and measures profile differences using a translated proxy implementation. The resulting profile signature gap is supplied to an agent for iterative refinement. We evaluate the method on Vortex, an open-ISA GPGPU, using robotics as the application domain. All active kernel pairs pass both output-equivalence checks, and the case studies show that iterative refinement can reduce profile distance.

title: Learning Social Influence with Unobserved Attention
summary: Social influence, the tendency of our social environment to sway our beliefs and behaviors, is often cited as a driver of population-level trends in opinions or beliefs. Many quantitative theories of social influence assume that an agent interacts with its entire social environment. This assumption is often unrealistic. For example, users of online platforms typically see posts from only a small subset of the accounts they follow at any given time. We introduce a simple probabilistic agent-based model of social influence that explicitly models unobserved attention mechanisms. The first of these latent mechanisms is selection: each agent interacts with only one other agent at a time from its social environment. The second is retention: the agent chooses whether or not to ignore the opinion of the other. Our model admits an efficient maximum-likelihood algorithm which allows us to fit it to opinion traces even when these mechanisms are unobserved. On synthetic data, omitting either latent mechanism reduces the overall strength of social influence governed by the inferred interaction kernel, which hides the evidence for the underlying nonlinearity of the social influence. We study a selection of previously analyzed empirical datasets and curate several new ones. We show that models that include the latent mechanisms are often more predictive on these datasets; indeed, they typically improve prediction far more than the choice of interaction kernel does. Modeling latent attention increases held-out predictive likelihood on 14 of these 15 datasets. Each mechanism changes the size of the inferred kernel in a predictable direction, while its effect on the kernel's shape depends on the data.

title: LEVER: Adaptive Cost-Aware Proof Search Over AND/OR Graphs
summary: Mathematicians value proofs for more than correctness: among correct proofs, simplicity, purity and the computational cost of finding them vary widely. Yet LLM-powered theorem provers largely search for any correct proof, and improve its quality only after it is found. We propose LEVER, a proof search algorithm that makes the objective over correct proofs programmable and optimizes it during search. LEVER scores partial proofs over an AND/OR proof graph, combining realized objective values with predictions for open subgoals, so the objective guides search before a proof is complete. The same mechanism optimizes computational cost, proof length, topical impurity, and even their weighted combinations, while the Lean kernel enforces correctness. On PutnamBench in Lean 4, under matched budgets, LEVER costs 34% less than a strong single-conversation agent while raising the solve rate from 80% to 96%. On reducing topical impurity, i.e., how far a proof strays from its theorem's subject, it improves over post-hoc refactoring (42% reduction against 33%) at two-thirds of the cost and more reliably; on proof length, the metric refactoring is built for, it approaches refactoring. Varying the objective's weights traces a quality-cost trade-off curve, so the user can choose how much a better proof is worth. Overall, LEVER is a performant, cost-efficient and tunable proof search algorithm for navigating the space of correct proofs.

title: Trajectory-Guided Fault Localization for Agent Skill Evolution
summary: Agent skills provide reusable guidance for code agents, but incomplete or unsuitable guidance can impair task execution. To reduce the manual effort of skill refinement, recent approaches use LLMs to generate revisions from execution feedback. However, grounding these revisions in explicit behavioral evidence remains challenging. To address this gap, we propose SkillMorph, a skill-evolution approach based on trajectory-guided fault localization in agent skills. Its core idea is to link execution evidence to specific skill contents before generating revisions. Specifically, SkillMorph compares failure and success evidence in abstracted trajectories across repeated runs and tasks, incorporating changes between evolution loops to identify suspicious actions. It then uses these suspicious actions to localize edit sites in the skills and generate corresponding revisions. Experiments on SWE-Skills-Bench and CannBot show that the skills evolved by SkillMorph consistently achieve higher trial-level accuracy and execution consistency than the original skills and those from four existing skill-evolution methods. We have also applied SkillMorph to automated kernel generation with an AI operator-development team, which has accepted 6 skill-revision pull requests.

title: Information Divergence and Endogenous Evolution of Asymmetric Information
summary: Standard theories trace information asymmetry to privately held information, heterogeneous signals, or costly information acquisition. We identify a distinct mechanism: otherwise identical rational agents observing a common Markov state at asynchronous times can hold different predictive distributions because their information differs in age. When the transition kernel separates information ages, independent Bernoulli observation arrivals make such divergence recur infinitely often almost surely, even with identical arrival probabilities. When agents instead choose costly updating intensities, independent update realizations can regenerate heterogeneous information ages among ex ante identical agents. In a stationary Gaussian AR(1) environment, the consequences depend on common staleness as well as the age gap: holding the gap fixed, older information raises individual uncertainty while reducing expected squared forecast disagreement and the value of certifying relative freshness. This generates stale consensus: low disagreement despite high uncertainty. With multiple ordered ages, costly certification supports partial-unraveling equilibria in which fresher types certify and sufficiently stale types pool. Under geometric information ages, more frequent updating weakly lowers the smallest and largest equilibrium disclosure cutoffs wherever positive-certification equilibria exist. The framework has implications for credit, insurance, financial markets, and multi-agent AI.

title: Kernel Autoresearch for Open-Ended Model Discovery
summary: Kernels encode the inductive bias of a wide range of machine learning models, yet automated kernel design faces a fundamental dilemma. A fixed grammar of base kernels and operators guarantees validity but limits the search to structures expressible by those building blocks. Conversely, unrestricted programs remove this limitation but no longer guarantee validity. In our stress tests, 22-58% of LLM-generated kernels that pass numerical checks on random inputs fail when evaluated at different scales or dimensions. We propose Kernel Autoresearch (Kernaut), which treats kernel design as open-ended model discovery. Coding agents write kernels as programs, while construction contracts ensure that every accepted kernel is valid. A quality-diversity archive retains high-performing kernels with distinct behaviors, and novelty screening steers agents toward functionally new candidates. Our experiments demonstrate that the discovered kernels encode reusable inductive biases that generalize to unseen tasks. On held-out black-box optimization families, a discovered kernel outperforms a meta-learned deep kernel trained on the same episodes. Furthermore, kernels discovered from ten enzyme-kinetic rate laws achieve lower error than tuned ARD and deep kernel baselines on five unseen mechanisms. The discovered kernels are also interpretable programs that human researchers can refine: a human-refined version of one further reduces the held-out predictive error by 5.7% and optimization regret by 7.8%.

title: SpecGuard: Proving a Task Is Broken Before the Agent Cheats
summary: As autonomous coding agents get increasingly deployed, the risk that accidental or adversarially injected misspecifications in tasks lead to dangerous agent behavior is critical to address. Prior work has shown that agents given such tasks rarely flag the conflict and instead cheat, editing tests or hard-coding expected outputs, and the actions taken to cheat can cause real damage, such as deleting a security defense to make a corrupted test pass. It remains unclear whether such conflicts can be established with independently verifiable evidence before the agent acts. We present SpecGuard, which detects and formally certifies these conflicts between task intent and tests. Given only the task description and codebase, SpecGuard autoformalizes the intended behaviour into a Lean 4 specification. The tests are formalized independently, and the Lean kernel checks whether any implementation could satisfy both formalizations, producing a machine-checked certificate when none can. On conflicted SWE-bench tasks, SpecGuard detects up to 72.8% of conflicts and formally certifies up to 51.1%, with a nearly five-fold lower conflict miss rate than model-based judgment. SpecGuard provides a pre-execution safety check that identifies reward-hacking opportunities through formal certification of task-level conflicts, before any agent behavior is observed. Our code is available at https://github.com/prmbiy/specguard.

title: SwarmReconGuard: Black-Box Detection of Distributed Collective Reconnaissance by Individually Benign-Looking Agent Populations
summary: Autonomous and agentic clients can distribute reconnaissance across many identities so that each request remains valid, low-rate, and benign-looking while the population collectively acquires broad system knowledge. We formalize this threat as Distributed Collective Reconnaissance (DCR) and present SwarmReconGuard, a reproducible black-box benchmark in which the defender observes only service-boundary telemetry. The Docker-isolated study evaluates 11 benign and attack behaviors across 10-10,000 virtual identities, comprising 440 test runs and 3,666,300 requests, with complete telemetry integrity. We compare semantic, Gaussian, conditional, graph, kernel, hybrid, and CUSUM-based detectors. Gaussian likelihood-ratio detection achieves 100$\%$ detection with 0$\%$ observed false positives on known attacks but only 3$\%$ on unseen policies. CUSUM yields 36.1$\%$ overall detection at 1.25$\%$ false positives, while hybrid CUSUM reaches 85.7$\%$ detection with 0$\%$ observed false positives at 10,000 identities. Results expose a major policy-generalization gap and motivate exposure-aware, scale-aware defenses.

title: Humanize: Judgement Engineering for Agentic Coding
summary: Agentic coding makes code generation cheap, but reliable completion remains difficult: the agent that writes the code is a weak judge of whether it is done. We present Humanize, a multi-agent orchestration workflow for agentic coding built around judgement engineering: explicit, mechanically enforced decisions at the boundaries between planning, implementation, review, and learning. A human approves a plan contract, a builder agent implements it in rounds, and a reviewer agent from another vendor decides completion; deterministic hooks, not a model, route work between these roles and enforce 72 mechanical gates. Viewed as a Markov chain over repository states, alternating builder and reviewer samples jointly from two models, so a defect survives only if both miss it. We study Humanize through its deployment, 118 public postmortems of real loops, and its applications. Over 68 versions in 108 days, it gathered 1,468 GitHub stars. Applications include a 567-file gem5 build-system migration under upstream review; Kernel Design Agents, which extend the loop with a kernel knowledge base and profiling feedback and placed in the top three of all three Full-Agent tracks of the MLSys 2026 FlashInfer contest; and, through Humanize Olympiad Agents (HOA), full scores in IOI 2026, IMO 2026, IPhO 2026, and IBO 2024, 418.5/437 in IChO 2026 (gold-medal). Humanize also achieves 672/672 on PutnamBench and ranks first (251/303) on Lean-Eval's leaderboard even competiting with professional mathematicians. The postmortems show that independent review catches unsupported builder claims, but stopping remains a key weakness. In reports that separate rounds by phase, two thirds of rounds occurred after implementation was accepted. This evidence is observational, not a controlled comparison of workflows.

title: Network Intervention by Polling Strategic Agents
summary: A planner in a network of strategic agents faces three entangled challenges: the optimum depends on agents' private information, queried agents may misreport to steer the outcome, and exact computation does not scale. We study these challenges in multi-activity network games with heterogeneous private technologies, in which the planner sets non-discriminatory prices. We show that the optimal prices admit a centrality-based decomposition of the welfare kernel: each agent's contribution scales with its squared centrality in a network reweighted by agents' preferences across activities. This decomposition motivates Poll, a polling algorithm in which the planner samples one agent per round, walks briefly through the agent's neighborhood, and updates the price from a local report. From the same decomposition flow three forms of efficiency: computationally, Poll uses significantly fewer operations than exact computation and other distributed methods, requiring up to three orders of magnitude less communication on a real-world network with over 300,000 agents; statistically, its query complexity scales with topology and preference heterogeneity rather than explicitly with population size; and economically, it converges to welfare-maximizing prices while admitting behavior-specific implementations that induce truthful reports and detect adversarial deviations.

title: Stateless Language Agents: Scaling Long-Horizon Automated Research
summary: Automated research systems increasingly run LLM agents over long horizons, but more inference does not by itself produce more progress: agents replay growing histories, duplicate one another's work, or stop experimenting while token consumption continues. Yet most evaluations use short budgets or benchmarks that saturate early, leaving these failure modes untested. We trace these failures to two choices: where research state lives and who decides what to try next. We introduce Stateless Language Agents (SLAs), built on the principle of stateful search with stateless agents: no agent carries its conversation across invocations; instead, the harness owns the research state (candidate solutions and measured outcomes) and reconstructs a fresh and role-specific context for every invocation. What each agent sees becomes an explicit design choice rather than a history that grows with the run. We implement this principle in the SLA framework, where a stateless Advisor reads harness-summarized evidence across search directions and assigns concrete experiments to parallel Workers. We evaluate SLA against three recent frameworks on software engineering, kernel optimization, and algorithm design at budgets of up to one billion tokens. SLA achieves the best final result on every task and reaches the strongest kernel baseline's final performance with over 84% fewer tokens. Ablations from shared checkpoints show that focused contexts and explicit assignments each contribute to SLA's progress, with effects that can compound over full runs, while the Advisor consumes less than 0.6% of tokens. These results argue for SLAs, which keep durable research state out of agent conversations, and show that short evaluation horizons can misjudge research systems and their components.

title: MemMux: Runtime Verification and Honest Resource Attribution for Fleets of Parallel Coding Agents
summary: Developers increasingly run a fleet of coding agents side by side on one workstation. Terminal multiplexers like tmux and a new generation of agent managers were built to arrange windows, not to govern memory. When ten agents each spawn language servers, test runners, and browsers, no standard tool can say how much memory belongs to which agent, confirm that a terminated agent's descendants are gone, notice a child that has escaped its agent, or keep the machine off the swap cliff when an out-of-memory (OOM) kill would silently discard uncommitted work. We treat these as runtime-verification problems: a hosting substrate should emit signals an operator can check while agents run. We present MemMux, an unprivileged local runtime (no kernel control groups) turning resource governance into checkable signals: per-agent attribution, complete reclamation, escaped-process visibility, bounded footprint under overcommit, and monitoring overhead. A claims-disciplined benchmark measures each against tmux and a raw-process baseline on identical workloads. Under a binding memory budget on a Linux host, MemMux holds the fleet under budget (7500 MiB) with zero swap by admitting a subset and reclaiming under pressure, while the ungoverned tools run every agent, pin the machine at its RAM ceiling (2x over budget), and spill about 2 GiB into swap. MemMux reclaims 100% of a terminated agent's process subtree where the raw baseline strands half of it (tmux matches us here; the raw baseline does not), and it is the only launcher we compare against that surfaces escaped children (10 of 10 detected). The cost: the always-on 1 Hz monitoring loop runs near 0.6% CPU at one agent but 2.7% at ten, above our 2% target. Running the harness on real Claude Code sessions shows 100% attribution and low overhead carry over to live agent trees. We release the engine, benchmark, and reproducer.

title: Evolving in Thought Space: Training a Small Model at Test Time Unlocks Better Discoveries
summary: Open-ended scientific discovery often requires repeatedly proposing and evaluating candidate solutions. LLM-based systems can support this process by generating and refining executable solutions from verifier feedback. Methods such as TTT-Discover use test-time training (TTT) to update the solution-generating LLM from verifier feedback, adapting its generation policy to improve subsequent proposals on the target problem. However, this becomes expensive when reliable execution requires a large model, since training must maintain gradients, optimizer states, and policy statistics while repeatedly generating long, structured outputs. It also complicates credit assignment: outcome-level verifier feedback must jointly evaluate the high-level strategy and its low-level implementation. In this work, we introduce Guidance-TTT, which separates these roles. A compact guidance model is trained at test time to propose high-level strategic changes, while a frozen execution model implements them as complete executable solutions. At each step, the system selects a promising previously discovered solution, proposes a change, executes and verifies it, and updates only the guidance model using an adaptive group-relative RL objective. This concentrates test-time learning on short strategic decisions while retaining the implementation capability of a substantially stronger model without adapting it. Without web access, Guidance-TTT produces strong solutions across four distinct domains: combinatorial optimization (Polyomino Packing), heuristic programming (AHC058), machine learning (Lasso), and GPU kernel optimization (TriMul). Across these tasks, it outperforms the best solutions reported in prior work while remaining competitive with state-of-the-art results on public online leaderboards. Code is available at https://github.com/Human-Agent-Society/reef/tree/guidance-ttt-support.

title: RESOLVE: Language-Agnostic Validation of GPU Kernels Through Testing, Reduction, and Proof
summary: AI systems can now write and optimize production GPU kernels, but validating them remains an important challenge. Evaluating the kernel on a few random inputs and checking that its outputs match a trusted reference kernel within numeric tolerances is not sufficient: races can cause nondeterministic behavior that fails to manifest in tests, and numeric tolerances can hide bugs and cause false positives even after extensive calibration. To address this challenge, we present RESOLVE, which combines testing and formal verification to build a comprehensive kernel validation pipeline. It operates in three steps: First, it tests for nondeterminism using binary instrumentation that perturbs execution timing to expose races. Second, an agent rewrites the candidate and reference kernels to obtain "reduced-concurrency" versions that are simpler to analyze but still produce bitwise-identical outputs in all tests.
